name: Complexity & Big-O
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: Measure and compare algorithm cost with Big-O: growth classes, loops, cases, space and amortized time.

lesson.intro: Big-O notation describes how the time or memory an algorithm needs grows as its input grows. It lets you compare approaches before you write them, and spot code that is fine on 100 items but crawls on a million.

sections.title: What Big-O measures
sections.body:
Big-O describes how the number of steps an algorithm takes grows as the input size n grows. It does not measure seconds, which depend on the machine, the language and the data. It answers a different question: if n gets 10 times bigger, what happens to the work?

Because Big-O is about growth for large n, you simplify a step count with two rules:

- Drop constant factors: 3n steps is O(n), and so is n/2.
- Drop lower-order terms: n^2 + 5n + 100 is O(n^2), because for large n the n^2 term dwarfs the rest.

This is why two O(n) functions can differ in speed by a factor of 10 in practice. Big-O tells you how each one scales, not which one is faster on a particular input. Strictly, Big-O is an upper bound, but people usually quote the tightest one they know.
sections.code:
def count_steps(n):
    steps = 0
    for i in range(n):          # n steps
        steps += 1
    for i in range(n):          # n * n more steps
        for j in range(n):
            steps += 1
    return steps

for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    print(n, count_steps(n))
# 10 110
# 100 10100
# 1000 1001000    the n * n part dominates: O(n^2)

check.question: What is the simplified Big-O of 5n^2 + 3n + 20?
check.explanation: Drop the constant factor 5 and the lower-order terms 3n and 20. O(5n^2) describes the same growth, but by convention constants are dropped. O(n^3) is a valid upper bound, but not a tight one.

sections.title: Common growth classes
sections.body:
From slowest-growing to fastest-growing, these classes cover most code you will meet:

- O(1), constant: indexing a list, a dict lookup on average.
- O(log n), logarithmic: binary search, which halves the problem each step.
- O(n), linear: one pass over the data, such as `max(nums)` or `x in some_list`.
- O(n log n): efficient sorting, such as `sorted` and merge sort.
- O(n^2), quadratic: comparing every pair of items with nested loops.
- O(2^n), exponential: trying every subset, or naive recursive Fibonacci.

The gaps are enormous. For n = 1,000, log n is about 10, n log n is about 10,000 and n^2 is 1,000,000. 2^n is a number with 302 digits, far beyond anything a computer could ever count to. Moving an algorithm down one class usually matters more than any amount of fine-tuning.
sections.code:
import math

for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    print(n, round(math.log2(n)), round(n * math.log2(n)), n ** 2)
# n     log n   n log n   n^2
# 10    3       33        100
# 100   7       664       10000
# 1000  10      9966      1000000

check.question: Which of these grows the slowest as n gets large?
check.explanation: log n grows very slowly: doubling n adds only 1 to log2(n). Every other option grows at least as fast as n itself.

sections.title: Analyzing loops
sections.body:
To find the Big-O of code, count how many times the innermost work runs as a function of n:

- One loop over n items with O(1) work inside: O(n).
- Nested loops multiply: n outer passes times n inner passes is O(n^2). If the inner loop runs over a different input of size m, it is O(n * m).
- Loops one after another add: O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) = O(n).
- An inner loop that runs from i + 1 to n still does n(n - 1)/2 steps in total, which is O(n^2).
- A loop that halves or doubles its variable each pass runs about log2(n) times: O(log n).
- An inner loop with a fixed number of passes, such as `range(10)`, is only a constant factor.

Watch for hidden loops. `x in some_list`, `some_list.index(x)`, slicing, `sum` and `sorted` all take time that grows with their input, so calling one inside a loop multiplies the cost.
sections.code:
def has_duplicate(nums):          # O(n^2): compares every pair
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] == nums[j]:
                return True
    return False

def halvings(n):                  # O(log n): n halves on each pass
    count = 0
    while n > 1:
        n //= 2
        count += 1
    return count

print(has_duplicate([3, 1, 4, 1]))  # True
print(halvings(1024))               # 10

check.question: A function loops once over a list of n items, then loops over the same list again in a separate loop. What is its complexity?
check.explanation: Loops one after another add: n + n = 2n, and dropping the constant gives O(n). Only nested loops multiply.

sections.title: Best, worst and average case, and space
sections.body:
The same algorithm can do very different amounts of work on inputs of the same size. Linear search finds the target on the first try in the best case, O(1). In the worst case the target is last or missing and every item is checked, O(n). On average it checks about half the items, which is still O(n).

When people quote a single Big-O without naming a case, they usually mean the worst case. Two common exceptions: hash table lookups are O(1) on average, and quicksort is usually quoted as O(n log n) average even though its worst case is O(n^2).

Space complexity measures memory the same way. Counting only the memory an algorithm adds (auxiliary space), a few variables are O(1), while building a new list of n items is O(n). Recursion counts too: a function that goes n calls deep keeps n stack frames alive at once, so it uses O(n) space.

check.question: Linear search looks for a value that is not in the list. Which case is this?
choices: Best case: it stops right away
Average case: about half the items are checked
It depends on whether the list is sorted
Worst case: every item is checked
check.explanation: A missing value can only be confirmed after comparing it with every item, so this is the worst case: n comparisons. Sorting does not help plain linear search, which never uses the order.

sections.title: Amortized cost and common operations
sections.body:
A Python list is a dynamic array with some spare capacity at the end. Most calls to `append` just write into a free slot: O(1). When the array is full, it allocates a bigger block and copies every item across: O(n) for that one call.

Because capacity grows by a constant factor (doubling in the textbook version; CPython grows lists by about 12.5% plus a few slots), copies get rarer as the list grows. The total copying over n appends is O(n), so each append costs O(1) amortized. Amortized is not a hope about typical inputs: it is a guarantee about the total cost of any sequence of operations.

Costs worth knowing for Python:

- O(1): `lst[i]`, `len(lst)`, `lst.append(x)` (amortized), `lst.pop()`.
- O(1) on average: `d[key]`, `key in d`, `s.add(x)`, `x in s`.
- O(n): `x in lst`, `lst.insert(0, x)`, `lst.pop(0)`, `lst.index(x)`, `min(lst)`.
- O(k): a slice `lst[a:b]` copies its k = b - a items.
- O(n log n): `sorted(lst)` and `lst.sort()`.
sections.code:
def copies_for(n):
    """Count item copies made by a dynamic array that doubles when full."""
    capacity, size, copies = 1, 0, 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == capacity:      # full: move everything to a block twice as big
            copies += size
            capacity *= 2
        size += 1
    return copies

for n in [1000, 1_000_000]:
    print(n, copies_for(n))
# 1000 1023
# 1000000 1048575    always under 2n copies in total: O(1) per append

check.question: In the doubling simulation, about how many item copies happen in total over 1,000,000 appends?
check.explanation: Copies happen when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, ..., 524,288, and those add up to 1,048,575, just over a million. Spread across a million appends, that is about one copy each: O(1) amortized.

keyTerms.definition: A description of how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
How the number of steps an algorithm takes grows as its input grows.
How the extra memory an algorithm needs grows as its input grows.
Cost that does not depend on the input size.
Cost that grows by a fixed amount each time the input doubles, typical of algorithms that halve the problem.
The input of a given size that makes an algorithm do the most work.
The cost per operation averaged over a whole sequence, which stays low even when a few operations are expensive.
An array that grows by allocating a larger block and copying items over; Python's list is one.

summary: Big-O describes how work grows with input size, not how many seconds code takes.
Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n^2 + 10n is O(n^2).
Nested loops over the same input multiply, loops in sequence add, and halving gives O(log n).
Say which case you mean: linear search is O(1) at best and O(n) at worst.
list.append is O(1) amortized, dict and set lookups are O(1) on average, and x in list is O(n).
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who does not program why a program that handles 1,000 items in 1 second might need about 17 minutes for 1,000,000 items if it is O(n), but about 11 days if it is O(n^2).

questions.question: What is the simplified Big-O of 3n^3 + 1000n^2 + n?
questions.explanation: Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop its constant. 1000n^2 looks big, but for any n above 333 the 3n^3 term is larger, and the gap keeps widening.

questions.question: Algorithm A takes 100n steps and algorithm B takes n^2 steps. Which statement is true?
choices: A is always faster, because O(n) beats O(n^2)
B is faster for n below 100; A is faster for n above 100
B is always faster, because 100 is a large constant
They are equally fast, because Big-O ignores constants
questions.explanation: n^2 is less than 100n exactly when n is less than 100, so B wins on small inputs. Past n = 100, A pulls ahead and the gap keeps growing. Big-O predicts the winner for large n, not for every n.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation describe?
choices: How an algorithm's work grows as the input size grows
The exact running time of a program in seconds
The number of lines of code in an algorithm
The fastest possible time on the best hardware
questions.explanation: Big-O is about the shape of growth. Seconds depend on the hardware and the language, so Big-O deliberately leaves them out.

questions.question: Which of these operations is O(log n)?
choices: Finding the maximum of an unsorted list
Looking up a key in a dict
Binary search on a sorted list
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the remaining range each step, so it needs about log2(n) steps. Finding a maximum must look at every item, O(n); a dict lookup is O(1) on average; sorting is O(n log n).

questions.question: Naive recursive Fibonacci, where fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2), is usually given which Big-O time complexity?
questions.explanation: Each call makes two more calls, so the call tree roughly doubles at each level and is about n levels deep. The tight bound is about O(1.62^n), but O(2^n) is the standard answer. Memoization brings it down to O(n).

questions.question: An O(n^2) algorithm takes 2 seconds on 10,000 items. Roughly how long will it take on 20,000 items?
questions.explanation: Doubling n multiplies n^2 by 4, so 2 seconds becomes about 8. 4 seconds is what an O(n) algorithm would take.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of f for a list of n items?
questions.explanation: The nested loops do n * n work and the second loop adds n, giving n^2 + n. Dropping the lower-order term leaves O(n^2). O(2n) would describe two loops one after another, not nested ones.

questions.question: Fill the blank so this loop runs O(log n) times for n >= 1.
questions.code:
count = 0
i = n
while i > 1:
    _____
    count += 1
questions.explanation: Halving i each pass reaches 1 after about log2(n) passes. Subtracting 1 or 2 takes about n or n/2 passes, which are both O(n), and i += 1 never ends.

questions.question: This removes duplicates but is far slower than expected on large lists. What is the problem?
choices: result.append(item) copies the whole list each time
item not in result scans the list every time, making the loop O(n^2); a set would fix it
The for loop visits every item twice
Returning a list is slow; it should return a tuple
questions.explanation: Each `in` check on a list is O(n), and it runs n times, so the total is O(n^2). Keeping a seen set alongside makes each check O(1) on average and the function O(n). append is amortized O(1); it does not copy the list.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explanation: The inner loop always runs 10 times, whatever n is, so the total is 10n steps, which is O(n). Nested loops are only O(n^2) when both loops grow with n.

questions.question: Quicksort is often called an O(n log n) sort. Which case does that describe?
choices: Its average case; its worst case is O(n^2)
Its worst case; it is never slower
Its best case; its average case is O(n^2)
Its space complexity, not its time
questions.explanation: With reasonable pivots quicksort splits the list roughly in half each time, giving O(n log n) on average. Consistently bad pivots make it O(n^2), which is why a single Big-O should say which case it means.

questions.question: What is the extra (auxiliary) space complexity of this function? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.code:
def running_totals(nums):
    totals = []
    current = 0
    for x in nums:
        current += x
        totals.append(current)
    return totals
questions.explanation: It builds a new list holding one total per input item, so the extra memory grows with n. The current variable on its own would be O(1).

questions.question: What is the space complexity of this function for a list of n items?
choices: O(1), because it creates no new lists
O(log n), because each call does little work
O(n), because n calls wait on the call stack at once
O(n^2), because each call copies the list
questions.explanation: Before any call returns, the recursion goes n levels deep, and each level keeps a stack frame. No lists are copied here (the index moves instead of slicing), but the stack frames alone cost O(n).

questions.question: Fill the blank so the duplicate check runs in O(n) time.
questions.explanation: A set gives O(1) average membership tests, so the loop is O(n). {} creates an empty dict, not a set, and has no add method. A list has no add method either, and even with append each `in` check would be O(n).

questions.question: Which operation is O(n) on a Python list but O(1) on average on a set?
questions.explanation: A list must compare x with its items one by one; a set jumps to the slot given by x's hash. Adding is O(1) for both (amortized for list append), len is O(1) for both, and looping over everything is O(n) for both.

questions.question: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it is full. What is the amortized time complexity of one append? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Full copies happen only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, and those copies add up to less than 2n over n appends. Shared across the n appends, that is a constant amount each, even though a single resizing append is O(n).

questions.question: Why does a dynamic array grow by a constant factor (such as doubling) instead of adding a fixed 10 slots each time it fills up?
questions.answer: With a fixed increment, a resize happens every 10 appends and each one copies the whole array, so n appends cost O(n^2) in total. Growing by a factor makes resizes rarer as the array grows, so total copying stays O(n) and each append is O(1) amortized.
questions.explanation: The fixed-increment copies are 10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n, about n^2/20 items, which is quadratic. The doubling copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, which is under 2n.
